{{Short description|Mathematical theorem named after Pierre Cousin}}
In [[real analysis]], a branch of mathematics, '''Cousin's theorem''' states that:

:If for every point of a closed region (in modern terms, "[[closed set|closed]] and [[bounded (set theory)|bounded]]") there is a circle of finite radius (in modern term, a "[[neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighborhood]]"), then the region can be divided into a finite number of subregions such that each subregion is interior to a circle of a given set having its center in the subregion.<ref name="h1">Hildebrandt 1925, p. 29</ref>

This result was originally proved by Pierre Cousin, a student of [[Henri Poincaré]], in 1895, and it extends the original [[Heine–Borel theorem]] on [[compactness]] for arbitrary [[Cover (topology)|covers]] of [[compact space|compact]] subsets of <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>. However, Pierre Cousin did not receive any credit. Cousin's theorem was generally attributed to [[Henri Lebesgue]] as the '''Borel–Lebesgue theorem'''. Lebesgue was aware of this result in 1898, and proved it in his 1903 dissertation.<ref name="h1"/>

In modern terms, it is stated as:
:Let <math>\mathcal{C}</math> be a full cover of [''a'', ''b''], that is, a collection of closed subintervals of [''a'', ''b''] with the property that for every ''x'' ∈ [''a'', ''b''], there exists a ''δ''>0 so that <math>\mathcal{C}</math> contains all subintervals of [''a'', ''b''] which contains ''x'' and length smaller than ''δ''. Then there exists a partition <math>{I_1, I_2, \cdots, I_n}</math> of non-overlapping intervals for [''a'', ''b''], where <math>I_i = [x_{i-1}, x_i] \in \mathcal{C}</math> and ''a''=''x''<sub>0</sub> < ''x''<sub>1</sub> < ⋯ < ''x''<sub>''n''</sub>=''b'' for all 1≤''i''≤''n''.

Cousin's lemma is studied in [[reverse mathematics]] where it is one of the first third-order theorems that is hard to prove in terms of the comprehension axioms needed.

== In Henstock–Kurzweil integration ==
Cousin's theorem is instrumental in the study of [[Henstock–Kurzweil integral|Henstock–Kurzweil integration]], and in this context, it is known as '''Cousin's lemma''' or the '''fineness theorem'''.

A ''gauge on'' <math>[a,b]</math> is a strictly positive [[real-valued function]] <math>\delta: [a,b] \to \R^+</math>, while a ''tagged partition of <math>[a,b]</math>'' is a finite sequence<ref>{{Cite book|last=Gordon|first=Russell|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1090/gsm/004|title=The Integrals of Lebesgue, Denjoy, Perron, and Henstock|date=1994-08-01|publisher=American Mathematical Society|isbn=978-0-8218-3805-1|series=Graduate Studies in Mathematics|volume=4|location=Providence, Rhode Island|doi=10.1090/gsm/004}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kurtz|first1=Douglas S|last2=Swartz|first2=Charles W|date=October 2011|title=Theories of Integration|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1142/8291|journal=Series in Real Analysis|volume=13|doi=10.1142/8291|isbn=978-981-4368-99-5| issn=1793-1134|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

:<math>P = \langle a = x_0 \leq t_1 \leq x_1 \leq t_2 \leq \cdots \leq x_{\ell-1} \leq t_{\ell} \leq x_\ell = b \rangle</math>

Given a gauge <math>\delta: [a,b] \to \R^+</math> and a tagged partition <math>P</math> of <math>[a,b]</math>, we say <math>P</math> is ''<math>\delta</math>-fine'' if for all <math>1 \leq j \leq \ell</math>, we have <math>[x_{j-1},x_{j}] \subseteq B \big( t_j,\delta(t_j) \big)</math>, where <math>B(x, r)</math> denotes the [[Ball (mathematics)|open ball]] of radius <math>r</math> centred at <math>x</math>. Cousin's lemma is now stated as:

:If <math>a \leq b \in \R</math>, then every gauge <math>\delta: [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^+</math> has a ''<math>\delta</math>-fine'' partition.<ref name="b1">Bartle 2001, p. 11</ref>

==Proof of the theorem==

Cousin's theorem has an [[Intuitionistic_logic|intuitionistic]] proof using [[Completeness_of_the_real_numbers#The_open_induction_principle|the open induction principle]], which reads as follows:

An [[Open set|open subset]] <math>S</math> of a closed real interval <math>[a,b]</math> is said to be inductive if it satisfies that <math>[a,r) \subset S</math> implies <math>[a,r] \subset S</math>. [[Completeness_of_the_real_numbers#The_open_induction_principle|The open induction principle]] states that any inductive open subset <math>S</math> of <math>[a,b]</math> must be the entire set. 

===Proof using open induction===    

Let <math>S</math> be the set of points <math>r</math> such that there exists a <math>\delta</math>-fine tagged partition on <math>[a,s]</math> for some <math>s \geq r</math>. 
The set <math>S</math> is open, since it is downwards closed and any point in it is included in the open ray <math> [a,b] \cap [a,t_n + \delta(t_n) ) \subset S</math> for any associated partition.

Furthermore, it is inductive. For any <math>r</math>, suppose <math>[a,r) \subset S</math>. By that assumption (and using that either <math>r > a</math> or <math>r \in [a, a + \delta(a)) \subset S</math> to handle the base case) we have a partition of length <math>n</math> with <math>x_n > \mathrm{max}(a,r - \tfrac{1}{2} \delta(r))</math>. Then either <math>x_n > b - (t_n + \delta(t_n) - x_n)</math> or <math>x_n < b</math>. In the first case <math>b < t_n + \delta(t_n)</math>, so we can just replace <math>x_n</math> with <math>b</math> and get a partition of <math>[a,b]</math> that includes <math>r</math>. 

If <math>x_n < b</math>, we may form a partition of length <math>n+1</math> that includes <math>r</math>. To show this, we split into the cases <math>r > x_n</math> or <math>r < x_n + \delta(x_n)</math>. In the first case, we set <math>t_{n+1} = r</math>, in the second we set <math>t_{n+1} = x_n</math>. In both cases, we can set <math>x_{n+1} = \mathrm{min}(b, t_{n+1} + \tfrac{1}{2}\delta(t_{n+1})) > x_n</math> and obtain a valid partition. So <math>[a,r] \subset S</math> in all cases, and <math>S</math> is inductive.
    
By open induction, <math>S = [a,b]</math>.
